To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

at 60 degrees but not at 2 degrees the helical propensites of the 20 genetically-coded amino acids, as measured by the NMR chemical shifts of the (13)C atoms of the carbonyl groups, are remarkably similar, and that the propensity assignments for the 20 amino acids at both temperatures are remarkably similar when made by using the ellipticity data.

at 2,25, and 50 degrees C, the propensity for a given amino acid residue to form helix is a function of temperature, and that the propensity for the residue to form helical conformations in water is context-independent.
the helical propensites of the amino acids are context independent, and that the propensities for all residues are temperature dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temperature-dependent, context-independent propensities of the amino acid residues to join preexisting helices.

the quantitative, context-independent helix propensities of individual amino acid residues, with their temperature dependencies, and with how these are to be incorporated into protein structure prediction algorithms.

the quantitative, context-independent, temperature-dependent propensities of amino acid residues to forego a random coil and join a helical conformation, and with the temperature-dependent, helix-destabilizing effects of charged residues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
helical propensies for the 20 coded residues and norleucines are context-independent, temperature-dependent, and can be assigned with high accuracy by NMR chemical shift data.
, at 25 degrees C, the propensity sets of this study are the most accurate available for predicting helicity of amino acid guests within Ala(19) host peptides.
the helical propensies of the amino acids are context-independent and temperature-dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the helical propensites of amino acid residues are strongly temperature-dependent but weakly context-dependent.
the temperature-dependent propensity set assignments reported here are accurate and precise, and are the best available for the purpose of modeling the temperature-dependent, helix-rich proteins.
the helical propensies of this report, assigned from NMR data, are more precise and accurate than those assigned from CD data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the helical propensites of amino acid residues are strongly temperature-dependent, and that the temperature dependence is context-independent.
the helix-breaking tendencies of residues are temperature-dependent and must be matched to the temperature of the system under study.
the propensity sets we report here are more accurate, and thus more reliable, for the purpose of helix prediction in proteins than any previously reported.
